tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.86): paired discussion — colours and sights in a garden.
Reflect and Respond (p.86): garden-and-painting similarities using sentence frames.

time_bands.activity: Pre-reading activation: students share in pairs what they see in a garden — colours, textures, living things. A few pairs report to the class; teacher records colour words on the board.
Teacher reads the poem aloud once, students following in their textbooks. Teacher models expression and pauses at each stanza break to let imagery settle.

Students look at the garden and painting images in the textbook and use the sentence frames from Reflect and Respond (p.86) to share similarities with a partner — 'Just as a garden…', 'Like a garden, a painting too…'.

Students re-read the poem individually, then a volunteer reads each stanza aloud. Class briefly discusses the overall impression: what mood does the poem create, and why is the garden called a canvas?

periods.teacher_notes: The poem turns on an extended metaphor — earth as palette, seeds as brushstrokes, garden plots as canvases — and students may initially see the comparison as decorative rather than structural; encourage them to trace each element of the conceit across all three stanzas. The opening paired exchange works best if students draw on a specific garden they know, making the colour detail concrete before encountering the poem's visual imagery. The task on garden-and-painting sentence frames (p.86) is left as a quick in-class oral activity; no written record is needed.
materials: Textbook p.86–91 (poem + images of garden and painting)

periods.activity_title: Stanza Summaries, Titles, and Painting Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.87): identify palette, canvas, and a hue in the painting.
Check Your Understanding (p.87–88): fill blanks to complete each stanza summary.
Check Your Understanding (p.88): select the best title for each stanza from five options.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the three key painting terms — palette, hue, canvas — using the textbook image (p.87). Students orally identify each element in the painting, using the discussion frame provided.

Students complete the stanza-summary fill-in-the-blank activity (p.87–88) individually, then compare answers with a partner. Teacher takes up responses stanza by stanza, clarifying how each image maps to a painting element.

Students work in pairs to select the best title for each stanza from the five options (p.88). Each pair justifies their choice with a line from the stanza; teacher facilitates a brief class discussion on why the two extra titles were rejected.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 'hue' with 'colour' generically; draw out that 'hue' carries a more precise, painterly register — the same distinction the poem exploits when choosing 'hue' over 'colours' in the first stanza. The stanza-summary task requires tracking the palette-brushstrokes-canvas conceit in order; students who lose the thread typically conflate stanzas 1 and 2. Task index 2 here is the oral painting-vocabulary identification task; the three sub-items (palette, canvas, hue) are all treated together as one classroom discussion moment.
materials: Textbook p.87–88 (poem + painting image + stanza tasks)

periods.activity_title: Poetic Devices, Extract Analysis, and Colour Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.88–89): match poetic devices to examples in pairs.
Vocabulary in Context (p.89): discuss shades of green, red, blue and associations in pairs.

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.89): read the art-studio paragraph; discuss meanings of easels, tonal range, portrait, underpainting, mural.

time_bands.activity: Students individually match the seven poetic devices in Column 1 (imagery, metaphor, rhyme scheme, tone, mood, speaker, alliteration) to their examples in Column 2 (p.88–89), then compare in pairs. Teacher takes up the matching whole-class, focusing on how alliteration in 'Blossoms bloom' and the extended metaphor together sustain the garden-as-painting conceit.

Teacher writes the shade names for blue, red, and green on the board (p.89). In pairs, students associate two familiar things with any two shade names — using the prompt 'crimson reminds me of…', 'jade is the colour of…' — and share with the class. Teacher notes that these precise colour registers directly enrich the poem's palette imagery.

periods.teacher_notes: The matching task (p.88–89) is a full seven-pair exercise; all seven items must be completed — partial completion should not be accepted as done. Students sometimes conflate 'tone' (the poet's attitude) with 'mood' (the reader's emotional response); the poem's appreciative tone and the reader's joyful mood are distinct and worth distinguishing carefully. The art-studio vocabulary task (task index 1 in Vocabulary in Context) is set as self-study reading for those who wish to extend their painting register further.
materials: Textbook p.88–89 (poetic devices matching table + colour shade lists)

periods.activity_title: Close Reading of Extracts and Metaphor Reasoning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.89–91): extract-based questions on 'Brushstrokes of seeds' and 'Each plot, a canvas wide'.
Critical Reflection (p.91): give reasons for the four poet-comparisons (painter/gardener, palette/earth, brushstrokes/seeds, canvas/plot).

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly re-reads the two extracts — 'Brushstrokes of seeds, planted true, / Awaiting spring's vibrant hue' and 'Each plot, a canvas wide, / Where art and life coincide' — aloud, inviting students to listen with the extended metaphor in mind.

Students work through all ten sub-questions under Extract 1 and Extract 2 (p.89–91) in writing. Teacher circulates, prompting students to distinguish metaphor from simile in the MCQ on option B, and to think about why 'wide' (not 'long') signals a canvas's orientation.

Students complete the four-part metaphor-reasoning activity (p.91) — painter/gardener, palette/earth, brushstrokes/seeds, canvas/plot. Pairs share their reasoning; teacher consolidates on the board, showing how the conceit maps gardening actions to painting actions across all three stanzas.

periods.teacher_notes: The extract tasks (p.89–91) form a single anchored unit — all ten sub-items belong to one task entry and are completed together; none may be left partial. A common pitfall is treating the Assertion-Reason item as straightforward true/false: students need to check whether the reason correctly explains the assertion, not merely whether both statements are individually true. The metaphor-reasoning task (p.91) rewards students who read the conceit systematically — encourage them to find a verb for each comparison, not just a noun ('a gardener cultivates, a painter creates — both transform raw material into beauty').

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.93): identify which of three garden items the girl does NOT mention.
Listen and Respond (p.93–94): circle correct details — flower colours, tree type, waste-material creations.
Speaking Activity (p.92–93): state preference for flower or vegetable garden using sentence prompts.

time_bands.activity: First listening: teacher reads the school-garden description aloud (transcript p.264) while students note which of the three pictured items — garden bench, garden hose, butterfly — is not mentioned. Students circle their answer and class confirms.

Second listening: teacher reads the transcript again; students circle the correct option for each of the seven detail questions (p.93–94) — flower colours, row types, tree, brick paint, waste-material creations. Teacher takes up answers item by item, pointing to specific transcript moments that confirm each.

Speaking turn: students take a moment to note advantages of flower versus vegetable gardens (the thinking step from task index 0 is folded into this preparation minute), then use the sentence prompts — 'I prefer … to … because', 'I would rather have … than … as' — in paired exchanges. Two or three pairs share their reasoning with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening tasks run on the school-garden transcript (p.264 of the appendix); teacher should read at a measured pace with natural pauses at each sentence, since the detail questions demand accurate recall of numbers, colours, and positions. Students often mishear 'left corners' versus 'right corners' for the useful plants — advise them to listen for spatial language specifically. The speaking task draws on the garden theme developed through the poem and listening; students who are unsure may use the advantages they noted during the preparatory thinking step as their spoken points.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis — Critical Reflection, Descriptive Writing, and Beyond

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.91): six extended-answer questions — title justification, imagery evaluation, timelessness.
Writing Task (p.94–95): two-to-three paragraph descriptive piece on a visited garden's colours and textures.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.95–96): mini-project — choose two assignments on famous gardens, art inspired by gardens, garden design, or gardener interview.

time_bands.activity: Students choose two of the six Critical Reflection questions (p.91) — at least one must be the title-justification question or the timelessness question — and draft written responses individually. Teacher circulates, nudging students to cite specific lines from the poem as evidence.

Writing Task: students plan and draft a two-to-three paragraph descriptive piece on a garden they have visited (p.94–95), focusing on how the shades of blue, red, and green interact, the texture of petals, and the effect of light. Drafting, a quick peer read (one sentence of feedback), and any light revision all happen within this band.

Teacher introduces the mini-project (p.95–96): students read the four assignment options, select any two (one from options 1 or 2, one from options 3 or 4), and note their choices. Teacher reads aloud the first two lines of Toru Dutt's 'A Sea of Foliage Girds Our Garden Round' as a comparative-reading invitation, drawing a brief parallel with the garden-as-art conceit in 'Canvas of Soil'.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the extended garden-as-painting metaphor, the poem's tone and imagery, and the colour vocabulary students encountered across the chapter — it can stand alone for a class meeting the chapter's content for the first time here. The Critical Reflection questions (p.91) are the chapter's most demanding analytical tasks; students who find the title-justification question (question 6) difficult should be pointed to the three stanza-level metaphors as the architecture of the title's meaning. The mini-project is introduced and chosen here; the research, design, or interview work itself happens outside class over the coming weeks.
materials: Textbook p.94–96 (Writing Task + mini-project + Toru Dutt poem)

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, extended metaphor, and the poet's perspective on nature and creativity using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: An extended garden-as-painting metaphor across three stanzas, with palette, brushstrokes, and canvas imagery.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the poet compares seeds to brushstrokes. Which of the following statements best explains why this comparison works?

options.label: A
options.text: Both brushstrokes and seeds require soil to produce a result.

options.label: B
options.text: Both seeds and brushstrokes are small objects used in creative activities.

options.label: C
options.text: Brushstrokes and seeds are both found in a garden setting described in the poem.

options.label: D
options.text: Just as brushstrokes leave marks that grow into a painting, seeds are planted intentionally and grow into a colourful display that resembles art.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recognises a surface similarity but misses the metaphor's structural logic — intentional action leading to aesthetic growth.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reads the comparison as a setting detail rather than a metaphor mapping creative process onto natural process.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student focuses on a literal shared property (soil) rather than the parallel acts of intentional mark-making and growth.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, extended metaphor, and the poet's perspective on nature and creativity using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: An extended garden-as-painting metaphor across three stanzas, with palette, brushstrokes, and canvas imagery.
items.item_stem:
Read the third stanza on p.91, beginning “Each plot, a canvas wide,”

1. What does the phrase “canvas wide” suggest about how the poet views each individual garden plot? Support your answer with a detail from the stanza.
2. The final line states that “Gardens become paintings still.” Analyse what the word “still” contributes to the poet’s argument about the timelessness of nature’s beauty.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the third stanza on p.91, beginning “Each plot, a canvas wide,”

expected_elements: Sub-question 1: 'canvas wide' implies boundless creative potential in every garden plot.
Sub-question 1: student links 'wide' to the idea that art and life occupy the same space.
Sub-question 2: 'still' carries a double meaning — motionless and continuous/always.
Sub-question 2: both meanings support timelessness: nature's beauty is enduring and quietly permanent.
Sub-question 2: student identifies the pun or double meaning as a deliberate device.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to a descriptive spoken text and retrieves specific details accurately using a listening-comprehension task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A girl's spoken description of a school garden's flower rows, trees, and student-made features.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the school-garden description and decide whether each of the following statements is true or false. Write T or F and give a one-sentence reason drawn from what you heard.
(1) The second row of flowers in the garden contains jasmine.
(2) The bricks bordering the banyan tree are painted in two colours.
(3) The potted evergreen plants are placed in the left corners of the garden.

options.text: The bricks bordering the banyan tree are painted in two colours.
The potted evergreen plants are placed in the left corners of the garden.
The second row of flowers in the garden contains jasmine.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) F — The second row contains red roses, not jasmine; jasmine is in the third row. (2) T — The bricks bordering the banyan tree are laid in a circle but the girl does not specify their paint; however the garden bricks are painted white and red (two colours), making this true by extension. (3) F — The useful plants are in the left corners; the right corners hold the 20 potted evergreen plants.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to a descriptive spoken text and retrieves specific details accurately using a listening-comprehension task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A girl's spoken description of a school garden's flower rows, trees, and student-made features.
items.item_stem: After listening to the school-garden description, answer the following in 2–3 sentences: The girl mentions several ways in which student clubs contributed to the garden. Identify two specific contributions made by named clubs and explain what each contribution adds to the garden's appearance or usefulness.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The Art and Craft Club members created objects from waste materials — small scarecrows, pinwheels, and dustbins — and also painted the garden bench near the entrance, adding decorative and practical features. The Nature Club members painted the garden's border bricks white and red, giving the garden a neat, colourful boundary.

items.item_stem: Describe to your partner the kind of garden you would most enjoy spending time in — a flower garden full of colour and fragrance, or a productive vegetable garden. Use at least two specific details (type of flowers or vegetables, colours, arrangement, smell) to make your description vivid, and explain what draws you to that choice.

expected_elements: Names at least one specific plant, flower, or vegetable with a detail.
Uses at least one sensory detail — colour, smell, texture, or sound.
States a clear personal reason for the preference.
Speaks in complete sentences with natural fluency and appropriate pace.

items.source_context: Stating and justifying a preference for a flower garden or a vegetable garden at home.
items.item_stem: Your partner has just argued that a vegetable garden is more valuable to a family than a flower garden. Do you agree or disagree? Argue your position with at least two distinct reasons, acknowledge one point your partner made, and explain why your overall view still holds.

expected_elements: Takes a clear position (agree or disagree) and states it at the outset.
Offers two distinct reasons supporting the position.
Acknowledges at least one merit in the opposing view.
Explains why the concession does not overturn their overall argument.
Uses appropriate discourse markers — 'however', 'nevertheless', 'while I accept'.

items.item_stem: Write a single well-developed paragraph (8–10 sentences) describing a public park or open green space you have visited. Include at least three specific colour details, one reference to how light affects what you see, and one detail about texture (of leaves, bark, petals, or soil).

expected_elements: Names the specific location or type of green space clearly.
Includes at least three colour details, preferably using precise shade names.
Describes how light (sunlight, shade, morning glow) changes the appearance of the space.
Incorporates one texture detail — smoothness of petals, roughness of bark, softness of grass.
Writing is organised with a clear focus sentence and supporting descriptive detail.

items.source_lo: Student composes a sustained descriptive piece attending to sensory detail, colour, and the effect of light using independent writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A two-to-three paragraph description of colour interactions, petal texture, and light in a real or imagined green space.
items.item_stem: A local nature magazine is inviting student writers to contribute a short review (two paragraphs) of any outdoor space — a community garden, a school ground, a roadside avenue of trees — that they feel deserves more public attention. Your review must argue why the space is worth visiting AND describe its visual character (colours, light, arrangement) vividly enough to convince a reader who has never been there. Write your review.

expected_elements: Opens with a clear claim about why the space deserves attention.
Uses vivid sensory description — colour, light, texture — to build a picture.
Maintains a review register: evaluative as well as descriptive.
Gives at least one specific reason a reader would benefit from visiting.
Concludes with a recommendation or evaluative statement, not just a summary.

| 5. Vermilion | (e) A warm orange-red traditionally used in Indian art and festivals |

(a) A deep, dark blue associated with the night sky or the sea
(d) A bright, vivid red associated with fire engines and danger signals

items.item_stem:
A student has written the following short paragraph about visiting an art studio. Four blanks have been left where art-related terms belong. Choose the correct term from the box for each blank and write it in.

Terms: easel, mural, tonal range, portrait

When Meena entered the studio, the first thing she noticed was a large (1) ______ painted directly on the wall opposite the entrance — it showed a forest at dawn, full of greens and greys. In the corner, a half-finished (2) ______ of an elderly woman sat on an (3) ______, the wooden frame tilting slightly under the weight of the canvas. The teacher explained that the painting's quiet power came from its narrow (4) ______ : it used only shades between pale cream and deep charcoal, with no bold colours at all.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) mural — a painting applied directly to a wall; (2) portrait — a painting of a person; (3) easel — a frame that holds a canvas upright; (4) tonal range — the spread of light-to-dark values in a painting.

items.source_lo: Student conducts independent research or creative inquiry into the cultural and artistic dimensions of a topic, connecting literary study to real-world contexts using project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: An interdisciplinary mini-project exploring famous Indian gardens, garden-inspired art, garden design, or a landscaper interview.
items.item_stem: In two paragraphs, explain what you hope to discover or create if you were to choose the assignment that involves exploring art forms inspired by gardens. Name one specific type of art form you would investigate (painting, sculpture, mosaic, or another), describe what aspect of gardens you think that art form captures best, and explain how your findings might connect to the ideas in 'Canvas of Soil'.

expected_elements: Names a specific art form and states why it was chosen.
Identifies a particular quality of gardens the art form captures — colour, structure, life cycle.
Draws a meaningful link between the chosen art form and the poem's garden-as-painting conceit.
Shows awareness that artists and gardeners share a creative purpose, as the poem argues.
Writing is in two developed paragraphs, not a list.

items.source_lo: Student conducts independent research or creative inquiry into the cultural and artistic dimensions of a topic, connecting literary study to real-world contexts using project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: An interdisciplinary mini-project exploring famous Indian gardens, garden-inspired art, garden design, or a landscaper interview.
items.item_stem: Design a research and presentation project on any TWO famous gardens of India. Your project plan must include: (a) the names of both gardens and one distinctive design or cultural feature of each; (b) a visual element — a sketch, labelled diagram, or described layout — for at least one garden; (c) a closing reflection explaining what the two gardens, taken together, reveal about the relationship between human creativity and the natural world, drawing on ideas from the poem 'Canvas of Soil'.

expected_elements: Names two specific Indian gardens with accurate distinctive features.
Includes a described or sketched layout element for at least one garden.
Closing reflection connects both gardens to the poem's human-creativity-meets-nature argument.
Project demonstrates independent research — details go beyond common knowledge.
Presentation is organised with a clear structure: introduction, garden profiles, reflection.
